x-e-e6-01.title: Sorting out the reasons for keeping a class pet
x-e-e6-01.topic: A short text and a simple opinion
x-e-e6-01.goal: In Jin's opinion text, tell apart the opinion itself, the reasons, the examples that serve as evidence, and the off-topic remarks, then judge in English which reason is the strongest.
x-e-e6-01.material:
Class 6-3 is talking about "Should we keep a class pet?" Here is Jin's text.

I think we should get a class pet. A pet can teach us to take care of animals. I like cats very much, and I want to see one every day. Class 6-1 had a fish last year, and students fed it by turns. Also, many students are afraid of dogs.
x-e-e6-01.thinking.0: Telling an opinion apart from the reasons that support it
x-e-e6-01.thinking.1: Telling personal taste apart from evidence that can be checked
x-e-e6-01.thinking.2: Comparing how strong the reasons are
x-e-e6-01.prereq.0: You can read opinion expressions such as I think ~ / because
x-e-e6-01.prereq.1: Easy words such as fish, pet, feed
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose every sentence that is a reason supporting Jin's opinion 'we should get a class pet'.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each sentence, ask yourself whether it helps the claim that the whole class should keep a pet.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.hint.1: Separate sentences that only show the speaker's feeling, like 'I like ...', from facts that other people can check.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.r.a: This sentence talks about a benefit for the class. Also compare it with the opinion: is it just the same thing said again?
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.r.b: Think about whether the speaker's personal taste is a reason for the whole class.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.r.c: This sentence uses something that really happened as an example. Think about how it connects to the claim.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.r.d: Decide whether this is a reason for keeping pets in general, or a worry about only some animals.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.r.e: Look at whether this sentence is a reason or the claim itself.
x-e-e6-01.s.s1.explain: a is a reason that names a benefit of keeping an animal, and c is evidence because it is an example another class really tried. b is only Jin's personal taste, not a reason the class needs, d actually speaks against some animals, and e is not a reason but the claim itself.
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences to Jin in English. Say which of Jin's reasons is the strongest, and give your explanation (or say what more is needed).
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one strong reason and take a word or two from that sentence to use in your answer.
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.hint.1: Use because or so to connect 'why it is strong'.
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say which sentence of Jin's text the reason you chose is?
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why that reason is strong (or what more is needed)?
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you judge the reasons for the whole class, not your own taste? (optional)
x-e-e6-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that points out the weakness of a reason (it has no example).

x-e-e6-02.title: Fixing the parts of an email to a teacher that do not fit together
x-e-e6-02.goal: Find where two lines of the email do not fit each other, and rewrite in English so that the plan works.
x-e-e6-02.material: Yuna is going to email her teacher, Mr. Park, about a group science homework meeting. The library can be used until 5 p.m. on Thursday.
x-e-e6-02.thinking.0: Finding contradictions between lines of an email
x-e-e6-02.thinking.1: Comparing possible fixes: which line could be changed
x-e-e6-02.thinking.2: Checking that the fixed sentence fits the other lines
x-e-e6-02.prereq.0: Reading a.m./p.m. and days of the week
x-e-e6-02.prereq.1: Easy expressions such as can, want to, after
x-e-e6-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in this email that does not fit the other lines, so the meeting cannot work.
x-e-e6-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put the meeting time next to the time when one group member can come, and compare them.
x-e-e6-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write down the day and the time of each line, including 'a.m./p.m.'.
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a meeting time between the earliest time Mina can come and the time the library closes.
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.hint.1: You can also change the day instead of the time. If you do, check that line 4 still fits too.
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Our group wants to meet...
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the time you fixed after the time Mina can come (or did you change the day)?
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does your fixed sentence fit both the library's 5 p.m. rule and line 4?
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does your fixed sentence connect naturally with the other lines in the email?
x-e-e6-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that changes the day and also makes the reason line fit.

x-e-e6-03.title: Is the book club a success? Changing your judgment as evidence grows
x-e-e6-03.goal: As data is added one piece at a time, change your judgment about the claim 'the book club is a success', and finish in English using two pieces of evidence.
x-e-e6-03.material: A new book club has started at our school. The teacher said, "The club is a success." You will receive the evidence one piece at a time and think about whether this statement is right.
x-e-e6-03.thinking.0: Not deciding from just one piece of evidence
x-e-e6-03.thinking.1: Changing your judgment when new information appears
x-e-e6-03.thinking.2: Writing a claim by combining several pieces of evidence
x-e-e6-03.prereq.1: Easy expressions such as sign up, only, come
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.prompt: Look at the data one piece at a time, and each time choose what you think about the statement 'The club is a success'.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.hint.0: Separate what the data you have now confirms from what you still do not know.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new data points in the same direction as the earlier data or the opposite direction.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.info: In March, 12 students signed up for the club.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this data alone, how would you see 'The club is a success'?
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.after: The number who signed up is evidence of a start. You need to see how they actually took part afterward.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is a success. 12 is a big number.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This reaches a conclusion from the number who signed up alone. We do not yet know what they did after signing up.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is not a success. Clubs are always unpopular.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This reaches a conclusion from a general statement that is not in the data.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We do not know yet. Signing up is only a start.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This states the limit of the evidence we have now.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Only 4 students came to the May meeting.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: There is more data now. How do you see it now?
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.after: Many signed up but fewer came. The evidence for 'success' has become weaker, but we still do not know why the number dropped.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The first number matters more, so it is a success.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This fits the new data to the first judgment.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The evidence for 'success' has become weaker.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This lowers the judgment by combining the two pieces of data.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a failure. 4 is too few.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: There is no standard for 'few', yet it jumps straight to a conclusion.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.info: The 4 who came read 3 books a month each. Meanwhile, 6 students moved to a sports club that meets at the same time.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now, what is the most suitable thought?
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Attendance dropped, but the students who took part read a lot, and the drop may be because the times overlap. We need to find out more before we conclude.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It dropped because the book club is boring.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 'Boring' is a reason that is not in the data.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The students who came read well, and the drop may be because the times overlap. We need to ask more.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This separates the facts in the data from what we do not yet know.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Only the 4 who came worked hard, so the club is a success.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This decides about everyone from the result of only some students.
x-e-e6-03.s.s1.reflect: At first it looked like a 'success', but your judgment changed each time new evidence came. You need to be able to change your judgment as evidence is added.
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences in English. Give your thoughts on whether the book club is a success, and include two pieces of evidence from the data above.
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write your thought in one sentence. (I think / I am not sure ...)
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.hint.1: Use but to connect a second piece of evidence (one of: attendance, books, the sports club).
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: I am not sure ... because ...
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you use two different pieces of evidence (signing up / attendance, etc.)?
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is each piece of evidence matched to the right stage of the data?
x-e-e6-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that gives both a part of the success and its limits.

x-e-e6-04.title: Making tables to find cases where the claim is true
x-e-e6-04.goal: Make several vote tables on your own for which the English claim 'it got the most votes, but not half of the class' is true.
x-e-e6-04.material: 20 students in a class each cast one vote for the activity after snack time: soccer, art, or music. The votes are called s (soccer), a (art), and m (music).
x-e-e6-04.thinking.0: Telling the difference between 'most' and 'more than half'
x-e-e6-04.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy several conditions at the same time
x-e-e6-04.prereq.1: The meanings of most, fewer than, half
x-e-e6-04.s.s1.prompt: The result was soccer 8 votes, art 6 votes, music 6 votes. Which sentence describes it most correctly?
x-e-e6-04.s.s1.hint.0: Add 8, 6, and 6, find what half of the 20 students is, and compare.
x-e-e6-04.s.s1.r.a: Check whether both conditions were confirmed with numbers.
x-e-e6-04.s.s1.r.c: Compare again whether 8 is bigger or smaller than 10.
x-e-e6-04.s.s1.explain: 8 votes is more than art (6) and music (6), so it is the most, and it is less than 10, which is half of 20, so it is not half. So a is correct.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different vote tables with a total of 20 students in which the same claim ('soccer got the most votes, but not half') is true.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.hint.0: Soccer must have the most, so start by choosing a value bigger than art and music.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.hint.1: Fix soccer at one value, then subtract it from 20 and split the rest between art and music. If soccer is too small, you cannot reach 20.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.ok.c1: Votes are whole numbers 0 or greater.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Write votes as whole numbers 0 or greater.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Soccer does not have more than art or music.
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.fail.c4: Soccer is at least half (10 votes).
x-e-e6-04.s.s2.explain: For soccer to have the most, art and music must each be smaller than s, and their sum is 20-s. If s=7, then a+m=13, so they cannot both be 6 or less, so it fails, and if s is 10 or more it is half. So s can only be 8 or 9.

x-e-e6-05.title: Can one wet umbrella tell us 'it is raining now'?
x-e-e6-05.topic: A hidden assumption in a simple claim
x-e-e6-05.goal: Find the premise that Mia's short reasoning believes without saying it, and make a situation in English where that premise is wrong.
x-e-e6-05.material: Mia said, "Dan came into the classroom with a wet umbrella. So it is raining outside now."
x-e-e6-05.thinking.1: Making a counterexample situation where the premise breaks
x-e-e6-05.thinking.2: Saying the conditions under which the claim holds
x-e-e6-05.prereq.0: Easy words such as wet, rain, outside
x-e-e6-05.prereq.1: You can read reasons connected with because/so
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.prompt: What is the thought Mia did not say, but must believe, for 'it is raining outside now' to follow?
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.hint.0: Go backward one step at a time from Mia's conclusion and see what is needed for 'the umbrella is wet' to mean 'it is raining now'.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.hint.1: Separate the facts already written in the text from the beliefs that are not written.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.r.a: This is a fact already in the text. Check whether it is a hidden thought.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.r.b: This is a general use of umbrellas. Think about whether it is a link this reasoning really needs.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.r.c: This talks about the bridge that crosses from 'wet' to 'raining now'.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a scene already written in the text.
x-e-e6-05.s.s1.explain: To say the umbrella is wet because of rain right now, you need the premise that there is no other cause. The umbrella can get wet even if the rain has already stopped, if the umbrella was washed, or if it fell in water.
x-e-e6-05.s.s2.prompt: Write one sentence in English about a situation where Mia's conclusion is wrong. Say why the umbrella is wet but it is not raining now.
x-e-e6-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think of things other than rain that make an umbrella wet. (water, time, place)
x-e-e6-05.s.s2.hint.1: A situation with a different time is also possible, like 'The rain has already stopped.'
x-e-e6-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In the situation you wrote, is the umbrella wet but it is not raining now?
x-e-e6-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you see why Mia's belief (there is no other cause) is wrong?

x-e-e6-06.title: Will Joy really be late? Choosing what to check and what to ask
x-e-e6-06.topic: A hidden assumption in a simple claim
x-e-e6-06.goal: Sort out what you need to know for the claim 'the bus is slow, so I will be late' to hold, and turn it into English questions.
x-e-e6-06.material: Joy said, "My bus is slow, so I will be late for school tomorrow."
x-e-e6-06.thinking.0: Telling information needed for the conclusion from irrelevant information
x-e-e6-06.thinking.1: Finding the two assumptions behind the claim
x-e-e6-06.prereq.1: The form of questions such as What time ~? / Will you ~?
x-e-e6-06.s.s1.prompt: What information do you need to check whether Joy's statement is right? Choose every suitable one.
x-e-e6-06.s.s1.r.b: Think about why you need the standard for being late and the arrival time.
x-e-e6-06.s.s1.r.d: Think about whether the claim rests on the belief that she takes that bus tomorrow.
x-e-e6-06.s.s2.prompt: Write one English question to ask Joy about what you want to check. (A question that gets the information you chose in s1)
x-e-e6-06.s.s2.hint.0: End your question with a question mark (?), and try starting with What time / Will you / Do you.
x-e-e6-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: If it is answered, can you tell whether Joy's statement is right?
x-e-e6-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your question clear in one sentence?
x-e-e6-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it asking for information, not stating a conclusion?

x-e-e6-07.title: Writing a reply that politely turns down a friend's birthday invitation
x-e-e6-07.goal: Sort out the parts a reply declining an invitation needs (thanks, a clear refusal, a reason, an alternative), and write it yourself in English.
x-e-e6-07.material:
Your friend Sam sent a message.

Hi! Can you come to my birthday party on Saturday at 2 p.m.? It is at my house. Please tell me by Wednesday.

But you have a family trip on Saturday, so you cannot go. Here is your first draft of a reply: "I can't come to your party. Bye."
x-e-e6-07.thinking.0: Comparing a vague refusal with a clear refusal
x-e-e6-07.thinking.1: Choosing the parts that care about the other person's feelings
x-e-e6-07.thinking.2: Writing yourself to suit the reader
x-e-e6-07.prereq.0: Expressions such as can't / thank you for ~
x-e-e6-07.prereq.1: Easy words such as Saturday, next week
x-e-e6-07.s.s1.prompt: Which changes would help turn the draft above into a better reply declining the invitation? Choose every suitable one.
x-e-e6-07.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine how Sam would feel on receiving it, and look for what the draft is missing.
x-e-e6-07.s.s1.explain: Starting with thanks and suggesting another day makes the refusal sound less cold. 'Maybe' makes it hard for Sam to make plans, and leaving out the reason can look careless.
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to Sam in two or three English sentences. Include thanks, a clear refusal (with a reason), and another suggestion. The reason does not have to be the family trip.
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write one sentence each in this order: thanks, saying you can't go, a suggestion.
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.hint.1: Use a clear word such as can't / cannot in the refusal, and connect the reason with because or so.
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does it include thanks, a clear refusal, a reason, and a suggestion?
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: After reading it, can Sam clearly tell "you can't come"?
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the tone comfortable English suited to a friend?
x-e-e6-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that ends by suggesting another day.

x-e-e6-08.title: Politely asking a teacher for a homework deadline
x-e-e6-08.goal: Compare how the same request sounds different depending on who is listening, and rewrite it as a polite request to a teacher.
x-e-e6-08.thinking.0: Choosing the way of speaking that suits the listener
x-e-e6-08.thinking.1: Changing a blunt request into a polite request with a reason
x-e-e6-08.thinking.2: Checking the parts of a request (title, request expression, reason)
x-e-e6-08.prereq.0: Can I / Could you ~? and please
x-e-e6-08.prereq.1: The fact that you speak differently to a friend and to a teacher
x-e-e6-08.s.s1.prompt: Which is the most suitable request to send to Ms. Lee?
x-e-e6-08.s.s1.r.d: Look at whether it speaks as if the result were already decided.
x-e-e6-08.s.s2.hint.1: Make the request with Could you / Would you / Can you or please, and connect a reason with We have ... or because.

x-e-e6-09.title: Rewriting a meeting notice for new friend Emma to read
x-e-e6-09.goal: In a notice that only close friends can understand, find the parts a new friend would not know, and rewrite it in English with the information needed.
x-e-e6-09.material:
Jun wrote this in the class group chat.
"BTW, we're gonna meet at the usual place after school. Bring the stuff!"

Emma, who just transferred into this class today, is in this chat too. Emma does not know the school well.

Please note: the usual place is the bench under the big tree next to the playground, and the stuff is a ball and water bottles.
x-e-e6-09.thinking.0: Telling apart what the reader already knows from what the reader does not know
x-e-e6-09.thinking.2: Checking that the message can be understood on its own
x-e-e6-09.prereq.0: Easy words such as place, bring, after school
x-e-e6-09.prereq.1: gonna is the spoken form of going to
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose every part that Emma would find confusing because she would not know what it is when she reads it.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.hint.0: Since Emma does not know the school well, find which words can be known only by people who have already spent time together.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.hint.1: Ask yourself whether each expression can be understood without an explanation.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.r.a: Some people may not know abbreviations, but if you work out the meaning, it may not affect understanding much.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.r.b: Only friends who have been together know where 'the place we always go' is.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.r.c: This is a general expression that anyone can understand.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.r.d: There is no explanation of what to bring.
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.explain: b and d are words you can know only if they were talked about before, so Emma does not know where to meet or what to bring. 'BTW' is fine to leave unexplained because not knowing it causes no big problem in understanding the meaning, so we accept both (including a is also accepted).
x-e-e6-09.s.s1.acc.0: BTW (by the way) is also an unfamiliar abbreviation to someone seeing it for the first time, so it can be fixed too.
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the message in two or three English sentences so that Emma can understand it too. Include specifically where to meet and what to bring.
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.hint.0: Replace 'the usual place' and 'the stuff' with the explanations you were given.
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.hint.1: Adding a greeting to Emma makes it warmer.
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Even if Emma does not know the school, can she find the place?
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can she tell what she needs to bring?
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does the tone make Emma feel welcome?
x-e-e6-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer in the form of an announcement to everyone.

x-e-e6-10.title: The same message about being late: how do you fix it when the reader changes?
x-e-e6-10.goal: As information about the reader is added one piece at a time, decide how to fix the text message, and rewrite it in English to suit the new reader.
x-e-e6-10.material: Jisu is going to write a text: "Hi! I'll be late. The meeting went long." Each time the person who will read this text changes, judge whether it is suitable.
x-e-e6-10.thinking.0: Knowing that what is needed changes when the information about the reader changes
x-e-e6-10.thinking.2: Writing a message that can be understood on its own
x-e-e6-10.prereq.0: Easy words such as late, meeting, arrive
x-e-e6-10.prereq.1: The phrase for introducing yourself with this is ~
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.prompt: Look at the information about the reader one piece at a time, and each time choose what would be good to do with this text.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.hint.0: First write down what the reader already knows (me, the meeting, the schedule).
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.hint.1: Find in the text what that person does not know.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.info: The person receiving it is Jisu's mom. Mom knows that Jisu has a school book club meeting today.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: What would be good to do with the text?
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Mom knows about the meeting and knows who is writing, so this short text is enough.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Think about whether the reader is someone close.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is enough to send it as it is.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This took into account what the reader already knows.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.info: Now the person receiving it has changed to Mr. Brown, a neighbor Jisu is meeting for the first time. Mr. Brown does not know Jisu, and they agreed to meet today.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.after: Mr. Brown does not know who Jisu is, what kind of meeting it is, or when Jisu will arrive. These three things need to be in the text.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This did not reflect that the reader changed.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Put in who I am, which meeting it is, and when I will arrive.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This tried to fill in what the reader does not know.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Use more abbreviations so it looks friendly.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: There may be more words the reader does not know.
x-e-e6-10.s.s1.st.2.info: Mr. Brown is an adult and came to Korea not long ago.
